summary: Documents a long-circulated unpublished draft that updated RFC 1036, the older specification for the interchange of USENET messages. It became the de facto standard for news article format. It was published in 2010, is historic, and was replaced by RFC 5536 and RFC 5537.

plainLanguage.summary: A rulebook for message-board posts that everybody followed for years before it was officially printed.

questions: what are control messages in usenet
subtitle: The format and procedures for network news articles, a de facto standard before official adoption.

tldr.problem: By the early 1990s, RFC 1036 was outdated and implementations diverged significantly, causing interoperability problems for USENET news systems.
tldr.mechanism: This document, informally called 'Son of 1036', specified the format for news articles (similar to mail but for broadcast), article headers, control messages, and propagation rules. It was circulated as an Internet Draft but never formally published until 2010.
tldr.outcome: This document became the de facto standard used by most news servers and clients for years. It is Historic because it was superseded by RFC 5536 and RFC 5537, but it remains significant for understanding the history of USENET.

today: This document is Historic. It was superseded by RFC 5536 (Netnews Article Format) and RFC 5537 (Netnews Architecture and Protocols), but it remains significant as the de facto standard that guided USENET implementations for decades before official adoption.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Network news articles are like email messages but sent to a newsgroup instead of a person. Rather than being delivered to a single destination, a news article is broadcast using a flooding algorithm: it propagates one copy to each interested host, typically storing only one copy per host. Network news originated on USENET circa 1980 as a way for communities to discuss topics.

RFC 1036 (published in 1987) updated RFC 850 to define news article format, but it became vague and did not match actual practice. This document, originally circulated informally in 1993-1994 as an Internet Draft (hence the nickname 'Son of 1036'), codified and organized existing practice while adding small extensions to solve serious problems.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a rulebook for how messages should look and behave on message boards. People used these rules for years even before this official version.

sections.title: Article Format and Headers
sections.content:
A news article is like an email message: it has headers (structured information) followed by a body (the actual message text), separated by an empty line. Headers consist of a name, a colon, and content. Continuation lines start with white space. Articles MUST have exactly one of each mandatory header: Date, From, Message-ID, Subject, Newsgroups, and Path.

The From header contains the poster's email address and optional full name. The Date header contains when the article was submitted. The Message-ID header uniquely identifies the article globally. The Newsgroups header lists which newsgroups the article is posted to (articles can be cross-posted to multiple groups). The Path header records the route the article took through relayer servers. Subject contains the topic of the article.

Many optional headers exist, such as References (linking to earlier articles in a thread), Followup-To (redirecting replies to a different newsgroup), and Control (for control messages). Non-standard headers should begin with X-. The body may be empty but ordinarily contains the message text, with lines limited to about 70-75 characters for readability.
sections.plainLanguage: Articles look like emails: a list of fields like 'From' and 'Date', then the message. They say who wrote it, what it's about, which message board it's for, and how it traveled.

sections.title: Control Messages
sections.content:
Network administrators use control messages to manage the news network without human intervention. A control message is an article with a Control header that directs relayers to take actions beyond filing and passing the article along.

Common control message types include cancel (withdraw an article from circulation), newgroup (create a new newsgroup), rmgroup (remove a newsgroup), ihave and sendme (facilitate article exchange between sites), checkgroups (validate which newsgroups exist), and sendsys, version, whogets (request system information from other sites).
sections.plainLanguage: Special messages tell the message-board network to do things like create new boards, remove old ones, or delete a message. Only authorized people can send these.

sections.title: Propagation and Network Processing
sections.content:
When a relayer (a news server) receives an article from a posting agent or another relayer, it stores a copy in its news database and passes copies to other relayers. The Path header is modified to record each relayer's participation in the article's journey.

Relayers must validate articles before accepting them. Key rules include: an article MUST have exactly one instance of each mandatory header; all article content MUST be ASCII; header lines and body lines MUST not exceed 1000 octets; articles MUST total at least 65,000 octets and SHOULD handle up to 1,000,000 octets. Relayers receiving invalid articles may reject them or attempt to correct obvious errors.

Articles are propagated according to the Newsgroups and Distribution headers. A moderator can be assigned to a newsgroup; in that case, postings are mailed to the moderator rather than immediately posted. The RFC also addresses gatewaying (converting news articles to mail and vice versa), message ID mapping for gateways, and administrator contact procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: As articles travel between message boards, each one that receives them adds its name to a 'Path' list, so you can see the journey. Rules ensure articles are valid before being spread.

sections.title: Compatibility with Mail and Character Sets
sections.content:
News articles are defined as a subset of MAIL message format (RFC 822). This means any news article is a valid MAIL message, so the same tools can process both. The RFC includes full details on how to handle non-ASCII characters using MIME encodings (a quick summary of MIME is provided in Appendix B). Non-ASCII octets in article content violate the standard, but cooperating subnets (groups of well-coordinated hosts) may relax this if they prevent articles from leaking to the wider network.

Articles containing non-ASCII characters MUST include MIME headers indicating which character sets and conventions are used. Posters are warned that trailing white space (even in body text) may be significant and SHOULD be preserved, though practices vary. The RFC also covers multiline headers, encoded words for non-ASCII characters in headers, and size limits.
sections.plainLanguage: News articles are basically emails, so they follow many of the same rules. If you want to use languages other than English, you need special MIME encoding so the board systems understand.

sections.title: Status and Security
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges security issues including potential for leakage (articles escaping from a cooperating subnet), attacks (forged articles, control message abuse), and anarchy (lack of coordination). However, the document does not provide detailed security solutions, leaving that to independent efforts. The RFC emphasizes robustness and backward compatibility as primary concerns: news software spans many years and hosts, so incompatible changes are impossible to roll out network-wide.

This document is Historic and was superseded by RFC 5536 and RFC 5537, which define modern USENET news standards. This version is preserved for historical interest and to document the de facto standard that guided implementations for decades.
sections.plainLanguage: The system can be abused or broken in various ways, but fixing those would require changing every board on the internet at once. So the document focuses on compatibility instead. Newer versions now handle security better.
